gloss: To look at something before it is finished or made public.
examples: You can *preview* the first chapter for free.
The teacher *previewed* the test questions with the class.
I'm *previewing* the slides before I print them.

gloss: To work out what something badly written or unclear says.
examples: I can't *decipher* my own handwriting.
She finally *deciphered* the doctor's note.
We spent an hour *deciphering* a letter from 1890.

gloss: To work out the meaning of something written in code or in an unfamiliar form.
examples: Children learn to *decode* words before they read fluently.
He *decoded* the message in under an hour.
She is *decoding* her grandmother's shorthand.

transitivity: both — transitive (scroll the page), intransitive (scroll down)
gloss: To move text or images up or down on a screen.
examples: *Scroll* down to the comments.
He *scrolled* through the article looking for the quote.
She was *scrolling* on her phone all evening.

transitivity: both — transitive (click the link), intransitive (click on the icon)
gloss: To press a button on a mouse or a spot on a screen to choose something.
examples: *Click* the blue link at the bottom of the page.
I *clicked* on the ad by mistake.
Stop *clicking* — the page is still loading.
contrast: You *click on* a link or simply *click* it; both are normal American usage.

transitivity: both — transitive (refresh the page), intransitive (the feed refreshes every minute)
gloss: To load the newest version of a page or a list.
examples: *Refresh* the page and the table will load.
I *refreshed* my inbox every five minutes.
The app is *refreshing* the headlines automatically.

gloss: To save a page so that you can find it again easily.
examples: *Bookmark* this recipe before you close the tab.
I *bookmarked* the article to read on the train.
He has *bookmarked* half the dictionary.

gloss: To mark part of a text with bright color, or to draw attention to it.
examples: *Highlight* every word you don't know.
She *highlighted* three paragraphs in yellow.
The review kept *highlighting* the book's weak ending.

gloss: To draw a line under a word or a sentence.
examples: *Underline* the verb in each sentence.
He *underlined* his name twice.
The editor is *underlining* the same mistake again.

gloss: To add notes to a text to explain it or comment on it.
examples: Students *annotate* the poem line by line.
She *annotated* the margins in pencil.
This copy has been *annotated* by three different readers.

transitivity: both — transitive (quote a line), intransitive (quote from memory)
gloss: To repeat someone's exact words in speech or in writing.
examples: Always *quote* the author word for word.
He *quoted* two lines from the poem.
She is *quoting* an article she read last night.
contrast: You *quote* the words themselves but *cite* the source they come from.

gloss: To repeat someone's words wrongly.
examples: Headlines often *misquote* scientists.
The paper *misquoted* her twice in one story.
He says he was *misquoted* about the budget.

gloss: To name a book, article, or person as the source of your information.
examples: You must *cite* every source you use.
The paper *cited* a study from 2019.
He has *cited* the same website four times.

gloss: To mention a source or an earlier text in your own writing.
examples: *Reference* the original study in a footnote.
The article *referenced* three other papers.
She kept *referencing* a movie I had never seen.

transitivity: both — transitive (paraphrase a passage), intransitive (I'm paraphrasing)
gloss: To put someone else's idea into your own words.
examples: *Paraphrase* the paragraph in one sentence.
He *paraphrased* the law for us in plain English.
I'm *paraphrasing*, but that was her point.

transitivity: both — transitive (plagiarize a paper), intransitive (students who plagiarize)
gloss: To copy someone else's writing and present it as your own.
examples: Never *plagiarize*, even by accident.
He *plagiarized* half his essay from a blog.
She was caught *plagiarizing* in her first semester.

transitivity: both — transitive (recap the chapter), intransitive (let me recap)
gloss: To go over the main points of something again briefly.
examples: Let me *recap* what we agreed on.
The host *recapped* last week's episode.
She is *recapping* the chapter for anyone who missed it.

gloss: To say or write something again, usually more clearly.
examples: *Restate* the question in your own words.
He *restated* his argument in the conclusion.
She is *restating* the rules for the new students.

transitivity: both — transitive (translate a novel), intransitive (the joke doesn't translate)
gloss: To put words from one language into another.
examples: Can you *translate* this sentence for me?
She *translated* the novel from Russian into English.
The letter has been *translated* into six languages.
contrast: You translate something **from** one language **into** another.

transitivity: both — transitive (interpret his answer), intransitive (interpret for the court)
gloss: To turn spoken words into another language as they are being said.
examples: She can *interpret* between Spanish and English.
A volunteer *interpreted* for the patient.
He is *interpreting* at the conference all week.
contrast: A person who *interprets* speech is an *interpreter*; one who *translates* text is a *translator*.

gloss: To write out in full what someone said or what a recording contains.
examples: I have to *transcribe* the interview tonight.
She *transcribed* the tape word for word.
The app is *transcribing* the meeting as we speak.

transitivity: both — transitive (dictate a letter), intransitive (he dictates to his phone)
gloss: To say words aloud for someone or something to write down.
examples: *Dictate* the address and I'll type it.
The doctor *dictated* her notes after each visit.
He was *dictating* letters all morning.

gloss: To add a written translation of the speech at the bottom of a film or video.
examples: They *subtitle* every episode in four languages.
The movie was *subtitled* in English.
A small team is *subtitling* the documentary now.

gloss: To replace the original speech in a film with speech in another language.
examples: German television *dubs* most American shows.
The film was *dubbed* into Italian.
The studio is *dubbing* the series for Latin America.

transitivity: both — transitive (conjugate the verb), intransitive (this verb conjugates irregularly)
gloss: To give the different forms of a verb.
examples: *Conjugate* the verb *to be* in the past tense.
We *conjugated* irregular verbs all week.
He is still *conjugating* them out loud in the hallway.

gloss: To write a word with a capital letter at the beginning.
examples: Always *capitalize* the first word of a sentence.
She *capitalized* every noun, as if she were writing German.
Days and months are *capitalized* in English.

gloss: To put commas, periods, and other marks into a piece of writing.
examples: *Punctuate* the dialogue correctly.
He *punctuated* the sentence with three exclamation points.
The letter was badly *punctuated*.

gloss: To join two words with a hyphen, or to break a word at the end of a line.
examples: Do you *hyphenate* 'well known' before a noun?
The editor *hyphenated* every compound adjective.
Her last name is *hyphenated*.

gloss: To make a word or a title shorter.
examples: You can *abbreviate* 'Street' as 'St.'
They *abbreviated* the title on the cover.
'Doctor' is usually *abbreviated* to 'Dr.'

gloss: To print or type words in slanted letters.
examples: *Italicize* the titles of books.
She *italicized* all the foreign words.
The quotation is *italicized* on page two.

gloss: To put words or names in the order of the alphabet.
examples: *Alphabetize* the list by last name.
He *alphabetized* his whole bookshelf one weekend.
The index is *alphabetized*, so it's easy to search.

transitivity: both — transitive (indent the first line), intransitive (indent before you start)
gloss: To start a line of writing further in from the margin.
examples: *Indent* the first line of every paragraph.
She *indented* the long quotation.
The paragraphs are not *indented* in this style.

gloss: To give each item in a list or a set its own number.
examples: *Number* your answers from one to ten.
He *numbered* the pages by hand.
The chapters are *numbered* in Roman numerals.

transitivity: both — transitive (rhyme 'moon' with 'June'), intransitive ('cat' and 'hat' rhyme)
gloss: To end with the same sound as another word.
examples: 'Cat' and 'hat' *rhyme*.
He *rhymed* 'silver' with nothing at all.
She is *rhyming* every other line.

transitivity: both — transitive (type a letter), intransitive (he types fast)
gloss: To write something using a keyboard.
examples: Please *type* your name in the first box.
She *typed* the whole essay in one night.
He is still *typing* with two fingers.

gloss: To type something again, usually to correct it.
examples: You'll have to *retype* the last page.
I *retyped* the address twice and still got it wrong.
She is *retyping* the letter with today's date.

gloss: To write out or reproduce exactly what is already written.
examples: *Copy* the sentence into your notebook.
He *copied* the quote wrong.
She is *copying* the file onto a flash drive.

gloss: To put text or an image you have copied into another place.
examples: Copy the link and *paste* it in the chat.
I *pasted* the table into the report.
He was *pasting* the same paragraph into every email.

gloss: To put something into a text in the right place.
examples: *Insert* a comma after the name.
The editor *inserted* two footnotes.
She is *inserting* the photos into the document.

gloss: To remove writing so that nothing is left.
examples: *Erase* the pencil marks before you hand it in.
He *erased* the wrong answer and wrote a new one.
The board had already been *erased*.

gloss: To remove text or a file from a document or a computer.
examples: *Delete* the last paragraph — it repeats the first.
I *deleted* the email by mistake.
She has *deleted* every draft but one.

gloss: To arrange how a text looks on the page or the screen.
examples: *Format* the list with bullet points.
He *formatted* the essay in twelve-point type.
The tables are *formatted* differently on every page.

gloss: To give something a new name.
examples: *Rename* the file before you send it.
They *renamed* the magazine last year.
The folder has been *renamed* twice this week.

transitivity: both — transitive (edit an essay), intransitive (she edits for a living)
gloss: To correct and improve a piece of writing before it is published.
examples: Could you *edit* my cover letter?
She *edited* the story down to 800 words.
He is *editing* the school magazine this year.
contrast: One *t*: *edited*, *editing* — the stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double.

gloss: To find the mistakes in something and make them right.
examples: *Correct* the spelling in red.
She *corrected* thirty papers last night.
The teacher is *correcting* our essays now.

gloss: To read a text carefully for mistakes before it is printed or sent.
examples: Could you *proof* this before I send it?
He *proofed* the newsletter twice and still missed a typo.
She is *proofing* the last few pages.
contrast: A short form of *proofread*, which is irregular: *proofread*, *proofread*.

gloss: To change the wording of a document or a law slightly.
examples: We may *amend* the contract next week.
Congress *amended* the bill twice.
The rules have been *amended* since you read them.

gloss: To say something again in different words so that it is clearer.
examples: Let me *rephrase* the question.
She *rephrased* the sentence three times.
He kept *rephrasing* the same idea.

gloss: To change the wording of a written text without changing its meaning.
examples: *Reword* the ending so it sounds friendlier.
The lawyer *reworded* one whole clause.
They are *rewording* the instructions for beginners.

gloss: To make a piece of writing shorter while keeping the main points.
examples: *Condense* the report to two pages.
She *condensed* the chapter into a single summary.
The article was *condensed* for the newsletter.

gloss: To make something easier to read or to understand.
examples: *Simplify* the language for younger readers.
He *simplified* the instructions after the first complaint.
This text has been *simplified* for beginners.

ru: составлять план (текста), набрасывать в общих чертах
gloss: To write the main points of a piece of writing in order before writing it out.
examples: *Outline* the essay before you start.
She *outlined* three chapters on index cards.
He is *outlining* his speech on a napkin.

gloss: To write something carefully, such as a letter, a poem, or a message.
examples: It took her an hour to *compose* the email.
He *composed* a short poem for the card.
She is *composing* a reply in her head.

transitivity: both — transitive (narrate a story), intransitive (he narrates beautifully)
gloss: To tell a story, or to speak the words that go with a film or recording.
examples: Who *narrates* the audiobook?
The author *narrated* her own memoir.
A child in the back row is *narrating* the whole movie.

gloss: To record something in writing or on film so that there is proof of it.
examples: *Document* every payment you make.
She *documented* the whole trip in a blog.
The changes are *documented* in the appendix.
contrast: The verb ends *-ment* (*DAHK-yuh-ment*); the noun ends in a schwa (*DAHK-yuh-muhnt*).

gloss: To add pictures to a text, or to make a point clear with an example.
examples: Small drawings *illustrate* each chapter.
Her sister *illustrated* the children's book.
He is *illustrating* a cookbook this spring.

gloss: To write things one after another in order.
examples: *List* the ingredients in the order you use them.
He *listed* every book he read that year.
The names are *listed* alphabetically.

gloss: To give a book, article, or piece of music a name.
examples: What should we *title* the article?
She *titled* the essay 'Small Hours'.
The album is *titled* after his daughter.

gloss: To write something down quickly and briefly.
examples: *Jot* the number on the envelope.
He *jotted* a few lines in his notebook.
She was *jotting* notes all through the call.

transitivity: both — transitive (scribble a note), intransitive (scribble in the margin)
gloss: To write something quickly and messily.
examples: He *scribbles* notes on the back of receipts.
She *scribbled* her address on a napkin.
The baby was *scribbling* all over the book.

transitivity: both — transitive (doodle a face), intransitive (doodle in a notebook)
gloss: To draw little pictures without thinking, usually while doing something else.
examples: He *doodles* through every meeting.
She *doodled* flowers in the margin.
I was *doodling* instead of taking notes.

gloss: To copy letters or a picture by drawing over them, often through thin paper.
examples: *Trace* the letters with your finger first.
He *traced* the map onto tissue paper.
She is *tracing* the outline in pencil.

transitivity: both — transitive (color a picture), intransitive (the kids colored quietly)
gloss: To fill a drawing with color using crayons or pencils.
examples: Let the kids *color* the last page.
She *colored* the whole sky purple.
He is *coloring* inside the lines for once.

gloss: To say or write more about something you have already mentioned.
examples: Could you *elaborate* a little?
She *elaborated* on her answer in the second paragraph.
He is *elaborating* on a point nobody questioned.
contrast: Takes *on*: *elaborate on an idea*. The verb ends *-rayt*; the adjective *elaborate* ends *-ruht*.

transitivity: both — transitive (contrast the two endings), intransitive (his style contrasts with hers)
gloss: To show how two things are different.
examples: *Contrast* the two endings in your essay.
The review *contrasted* her new novel with her first.
He is *contrasting* American and British spelling.
contrast: The verb is *kuhn-TRAST*; the noun is *KAHN-trast*.

gloss: To tell or write the story of something that happened.
examples: *Recount* the events in the order they happened.
He *recounted* the whole argument to his brother.
She is *recounting* her first year in Chicago.

gloss: To describe or show a person or place in a particular way in a book or film.
examples: The novel *portrays* a small town in winter.
She *portrayed* her father as a hero.
Teachers are often *portrayed* as saints in these books.

gloss: To show or describe something in words or pictures.
examples: The article *depicts* life in a border town.
The painting *depicted* a harvest.
Poverty is rarely *depicted* honestly on television.

transitivity: both — transitive (print a copy), intransitive (the printer isn't printing)
gloss: To put words or pictures on paper with a machine, or to publish them.
examples: *Print* two copies for the meeting.
The paper *printed* a correction the next day.
The book is being *printed* this month.
contrast: It also means writing in separate letters: *Print your name clearly.*

gloss: To print a book or an article again.
examples: They will *reprint* the novel with a new cover.
The magazine *reprinted* her essay in June.
The book has been *reprinted* eleven times.

gloss: To make a paper copy of a page with a machine.
examples: *Photocopy* your passport and keep it somewhere safe.
She *photocopied* the whole chapter for the class.
He is *photocopying* the forms now.

gloss: To copy a document or photograph into a computer with a machine.
examples: Can you *scan* the contract and email it?
I *scanned* all the old family photographs.
The library is *scanning* its oldest books.

gloss: To send a copy of a document over a phone line.
examples: The clinic asks you to *fax* the form.
She *faxed* the signed page this morning.
Doctors are still *faxing* prescriptions to pharmacies.

gloss: To make an exact copy of something.
examples: *Duplicate* the file before you edit it.
She *duplicated* the handout for the whole class.
The slides are being *duplicated* for everyone.
contrast: The verb ends *-kayt*; the noun and adjective end *-kuht* (*a duplicate copy*).

transitivity: both — transitive (publish a novel), intransitive (publish or perish)
gloss: To make a piece of writing available to readers, in print or online.
examples: Small presses *publish* most poetry.
She *published* her first novel at forty.
The results have not been *published* yet.

gloss: To publish a text again, often in a new form.
examples: They plan to *republish* her diaries next fall.
The essay was *republished* online a week later.
A university press is *republishing* his early novels.

transitivity: both — transitive (circulate a draft), intransitive (rumors circulate)
gloss: To pass something around so that many people see it.
examples: *Circulate* the draft before Friday.
Someone *circulated* the memo to the whole office.
Rumors were *circulating* long before the article appeared.

gloss: To cut out parts of a text, film, or letter that someone in authority finds unacceptable.
examples: Some governments *censor* the news.
The prison *censored* his letters.
Whole pages had been *censored* before the file was released.
contrast: *Censor* (cut out) is not *censure* (criticize officially) or *sensor* (a device).

gloss: To black out parts of a document before it is made public.
examples: They *redact* names to protect privacy.
The agency *redacted* half the report.
The emails were released in *redacted* form.

gloss: To take back something you said or published because it was wrong.
examples: The paper had to *retract* the story.
He *retracted* the statement the next day.
Two of the study's claims have been *retracted*.

gloss: To give a story, person, or work a prominent place in a publication or program.
examples: The magazine *features* a new poet every month.
They *featured* her essay on the front page.
The issue *featuring* the interview sold out.

transitivity: both — transitive (pitch a story), intransitive (pitch to an editor)
gloss: To offer an idea for a story, book, or project to someone who might buy it.
examples: *Pitch* the story to an editor first.
She *pitched* three articles and sold two.
He is *pitching* his novel to agents this month.

gloss: To rewrite a book or story so that it can be a film, a play, or a version for other readers.
examples: They plan to *adapt* the novel for television.
She *adapted* the play for young audiences.
The book has been *adapted* three times already.
contrast: *Adapt* (change something) is not *adopt* (take as your own).

gloss: To report on a subject or an event for a newspaper, website, or channel.
examples: She *covers* city hall for the local paper.
Reporters *covered* the trial for six weeks.
He is *covering* the election this year.

transitivity: both — transitive (review a novel), intransitive (she reviews for the paper)
gloss: To write a published opinion of a book, film, or restaurant.
examples: She *reviews* mysteries for a small paper.
The Times *reviewed* his novel twice.
The film has been *reviewed* everywhere.

gloss: To judge a piece of work carefully and say what is good and bad about it.
examples: Classmates *critique* each other's drafts.
The professor *critiqued* my argument line by line.
They spent the hour *critiquing* the opening chapter.

gloss: To judge how good something is, often by giving it stars or points.
examples: Readers *rate* the book four stars out of five.
She *rated* the hotel poorly in her review.
The app is *rated* for ages twelve and up.

transitivity: both — transitive (upload a file), intransitive (it's still uploading)
gloss: To send a file from your own device to the internet or a server.
examples: *Upload* the essay before midnight.
He *uploaded* the wrong version by mistake.
She is *uploading* the photos now.

transitivity: both — transitive (download a book), intransitive (the file is downloading)
gloss: To copy a file from the internet onto your own device.
examples: *Download* the form and print it.
I *downloaded* the book last night.
The article can be *downloaded* free.

gloss: To send a file together with an email or a letter.
examples: *Attach* your résumé to the email.
She *attached* the wrong photo.
A copy of the contract is *attached* below.
contrast: Third person adds *-es*: *attaches*. You attach a file **to** a message.

gloss: To store documents or messages for the long term instead of deleting them.
examples: *Archive* the old emails instead of deleting them.
The library *archived* every issue of the paper.
Her letters have been *archived* at the university.

gloss: To put together a book, list, or report out of many separate pieces.
examples: They *compile* a new dictionary every decade.
She *compiled* his poems into one volume.
He is *compiling* a list of sources.

gloss: To list things in order so that they can be found again.
examples: Volunteers *catalog* the donated books.
She *cataloged* the whole collection in a month.
The photographs are being *cataloged* by year.

gloss: To write down events, hours, or numbers in an official record.
examples: Drivers *log* every trip they make.
The nurse *logged* his temperature at noon.
She has been *logging* her reading all year.

gloss: To mark something so that someone will notice it and deal with it.
examples: *Flag* any sentence you don't understand.
The editor *flagged* three factual errors.
Two emails are *flagged* as urgent.

gloss: To attach a name or a keyword to a photo, post, or file.
examples: Don't *tag* me in that photo.
She *tagged* the post with three keywords.
He is *tagging* everyone who was there.

gloss: To write a short line of text under a photograph or a picture.
examples: *Caption* each photo with a name and a date.
She *captioned* the picture 'First day of school'.
All the videos are *captioned* for deaf viewers.

transitivity: both — transitive (message a friend), intransitive (we messaged all night)
gloss: To send someone a written message online or on a phone.
examples: *Message* me when you land.
He *messaged* her three times before she answered.
She is *messaging* the whole group now.

gloss: To write regularly on a personal website.
examples: She *blogs* about teaching English.
He *blogged* every single day for a year.
They have been *blogging* since college.

gloss: To publish someone else's post again on your own page.
examples: Feel free to *repost* the announcement.
Hundreds of people *reposted* the article.
She is *reposting* it with a comment of her own.

transitivity: both — transitive (sign a letter), intransitive (sign at the bottom)
gloss: To write your name on a document to show that it is yours or that you agree.
examples: *Sign* at the bottom of the second page.
She *signed* the lease yesterday.
The letter came back because it wasn't *signed*.

gloss: To sign your name on something for someone who admires your work.
examples: Writers often *autograph* books after a reading.
He *autographed* my copy of the novel.
She is *autographing* posters in the lobby.

gloss: To write a short personal message in a book or on an object.
examples: Authors sometimes *inscribe* books for their readers.
She *inscribed* the copy to her old teacher.
The ring is *inscribed* with a date.

gloss: To write your initials on a document to show you have read or approved it.
examples: *Initial* each page of the contract.
She *initialed* the changes in the margin.
Every correction has been *initialed* by the manager.

gloss: To write the day's date on a document.
examples: Sign and *date* the form at the bottom.
He *dated* the letter March 3.
The check was *dated* last year, so the bank refused it.
contrast: The same verb also means 'go out with someone': *They dated for two years.*

gloss: To write on an envelope or a package where it should be sent.
examples: *Address* the envelope in block letters.
She *addressed* a hundred invitations by hand.
The package was *addressed* to my old apartment.
contrast: The verb is always *uh-DRES*; Americans often say the noun as *AD-res*.

gloss: To press an official mark onto a document, or to put a postage stamp on a letter.
examples: The clerk will *stamp* your copy.
They *stamped* my passport at the border.
Send a *stamped*, self-addressed envelope.

gloss: To put something into an envelope together with a letter.
examples: Please *enclose* a copy of your ID.
She *enclosed* a check with the form.
A return envelope is *enclosed*.

gloss: To sign the back of a check, or to say publicly in writing that you support someone.
examples: You have to *endorse* the check before you deposit it.
The paper *endorsed* her for mayor.
The book is *endorsed* by two famous novelists.

gloss: To state officially, usually in writing, that something is true or correct.
examples: A translator must *certify* the translation.
The clerk *certified* the copy for a small fee.
The documents have been *certified* by a notary.

gloss: To have a document officially witnessed and stamped by a notary.
examples: The bank can *notarize* the letter for you.
They *notarized* the agreement downtown.
The form must be signed and *notarized*.

transitivity: both — transitive (check your spelling), intransitive (check before you send it)
gloss: To look at something carefully to make sure it is correct.
examples: *Check* your spelling before you print it.
She *checked* the figures twice.
He is *checking* the references at the back.

transitivity: both — transitive (grade the essays), intransitive (she grades on weekends)
gloss: To read students' work and give it a score or a letter.
examples: Teachers *grade* essays on the weekend.
He *graded* forty papers last night.
The exams are being *graded* this week.

transitivity: both — transitive (score the tests), intransitive (she scored well)
gloss: To give a test or a piece of work a number of points, or to earn those points.
examples: Two readers *score* each essay.
She *scored* well on the reading section.
The tests are *scored* by computer.

gloss: To ask someone a set of short questions to test what they know.
examples: *Quiz* me on the new vocabulary.
The teacher *quizzed* us on chapter four.
She was *quizzing* her son on the state capitals.

transitivity: both — transitive (practice your handwriting), intransitive (practice every day)
gloss: To do something again and again in order to get better at it.
examples: *Practice* reading out loud.
He *practiced* his handwriting every evening.
She has been *practicing* her English on the phone.
contrast: American spelling is *practice* for both noun and verb; British spells the verb *practise*.

gloss: To draw a ring around a word or a number.
examples: *Circle* the correct answer.
She *circled* two typos on the first page.
He is *circling* the dates on the calendar.

ru: писать очерк о ком-либо, делать портрет (в прессе)
gloss: To write a long article describing a person's life and work.
examples: The magazine *profiles* one scientist a month.
She *profiled* the mayor last spring.
He is being *profiled* in Sunday's paper.

gloss: To make a book or a speech shorter by cutting parts of it out.
examples: Publishers often *abridge* long classics for students.
They *abridged* the novel for the audiobook.
I'd rather read the unabridged version than an *abridged* one.

gloss: To show clearly in writing that something is important.
examples: These numbers *underscore* how much reading has changed.
The article *underscored* the danger of copying without citing.
Her letter is *underscoring* a point the report ignored.
